1208.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ (“dog”). Cognates include Latin canis, Sanskrit श्वन् (śván) and Old English hund (English hound).

1273.t: Perhaps related to μαδάω (madáō, “to be moist”). If so, then from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“wet; glossy; fat; well-fed”).

1263.t: Etymology tree Proto-Semitic *bayt- Biblical Hebrew בֵּית (bet) Biblical Hebrew לֶחֶם (lékhem) Biblical Hebrew בֵּית לֶחֶם (bêṯ leḥem)bor. Ancient Greek Βηθλεέμ Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew בֵּית לֶחֶם (bêṯ leḥem).

1247.t: From Proto-Hellenic *klépt͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *klép-ye-ti, from *klep-. Cognates include Latin clepō and Gothic 𐌷𐌻𐌹𐍆𐌰𐌽 (hlifan).

1201.t: From Phoenician 𐤑𐤓 (ṣr), cognate with Biblical Hebrew צוֹר (ṣôr) and Aramaic טור.

1284.t: From Proto-Hellenic *táuros, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros; cognates include Latin taurus, Lithuanian taũras, Old English stēor (English steer), and Albanian ter.

1223.t: Of Semitic origin; compare Biblical Hebrew אֱדוֹם (ʾĕḏôm).

1269.t: Traditionally related to δέρκομαι (dérkomai, “to see”) with the literal meaning of “one who stares” or, alternatively, “sharp-sighted”.

1224.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *díkā, from Proto-Indo-European *díḱeh₂, from the root *deyḱ- (“to point, show”). Closely related to δείκνυμι (deíknūmĭ, “to show”).

1299.t: From Proto-Hellenic *gumnós (with Cowgill's Law: o → u between labial and resonant), from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷnós by metathesis (possible taboo deformation; if the metathesis didn't happen we would have *νυγνός (*nugnós)), from *nogʷós (“naked”).

1268.t: Back-formation from δάκρυα (dắkrŭă), the nominative plural of δάκρυ (dắkrŭ).

1240.t: From some derivation from Proto-Indo-European *h₃érō, whence also ὄρνις (órnis). Cognates include Old Armenian որոր (oror), Hittite 𒄩𒀀𒊏𒀸 (ḫāras), Proto-Slavic *orьlъ, and Old English earn (English erne).

1210.t: Uncertain. Has traditionally been connected with νήχω (nḗkhō, “to swim”) from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂- (“to flow, to swim”).

1276.t: Of unclear origin. Traditionally compared with Sanskrit मूर (mūrá, “dull, stupid, foolish”), from Proto-Indo-European *mowHrós, *muHrós (“dull, stupid”), with ablaut *ō(u) : *ū.

1255.t: Together with Mycenaean Greek 𐀑𐀵 (ki-to) and likely Latin tunica, from some Central Semitic, as found in Aramaic כִּיתּוּנָא (kittōnā, “tunic”) / ܟܝܬܘܢܐ (kittōnā, “tunic”), Hebrew כֻּתֹּנֶת (kuttṓnĕṯ, “tunic”), which is derived from the local word for…

1275.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mḗros, of uncertain ultimate origin. Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *mḗms, *mēms-rom (“flesh”).

1286.t: According to Beekes, probably from Pre-Greek or some other language, based on the interchange of suffixes in the Mycenaean cognates.

1252.t: From Proto-Hellenic *prā́t͏̌t͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥h₂-k-yé-ti, a *k-enlargement of *per- (“to go over, cross”).

1218.t: From ἀπο- (apo-, “off”) + ὁρίζω (horĭ́zō, “separate”), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”) + -ίζω (-ízō, denominative verb suffix).

1234.t: From the root of ἁμαρτάνω (hamartánō, “I miss, fail, am deprived of (a thing), fail to do, sin”) + -μα (-ma, “instance of”).

1266.t: Ultimately from γέρων (gérōn, “old man”). Related to Mycenaean Greek 𐀐𐀫𐀯𐀊 (ke-ro-si-ja)

1246.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁wes- Proto-Indo-European *-us Proto-Indo-European *h₁wésus? Proto-Indo-European *h₁es-? Proto-Indo-European *h₁su- Proto-Hellenic *ehu- Ancient Greek ἐΰς (eǘs) Ancient Greek εὖ (eû) Ancient Greek εὐ- (eu-)…

1295.t: Of Pre-Greek or other Mediterranean substrate origin and possibly related to Latin vaccinium. Note the Pre-Greek suffix -ινθ- (-inth-).

1227.t: Appears to be related to πρό (pró), Latin prior, priscus and Lithuanian prie, but the exact formation is uncertain. Perhaps from an old locative *pr-i of Proto-Indo-European *pró (“forward”).

1222.t: From Proto-Indo-European *selk- (“to pull, draw”). Cognate with Latin sulcus (“furrow, groove”), Old English sulh (“plow”), Albanian hulli (“furrow”).

1228.t: Uncertain: * Furnée connects ἄσβολος (ásbolos, “soot”) and σπολεύς (spoleús, “loaf”), the former with a prothetic vowel α- (a-), and both showing a variation δ ~ λ (d ~ l).

1267.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ǵērh₂-s, a lengthened-grade derivative of *ǵerh₂- (“to grow old”). Cognate with Sanskrit जरा (jarā́, “old age”).

1217.t: Arcadocypriot Greek καταρϝος (katarwos, “cursed”) suggests a preform Proto-Hellenic *arwā, which makes Attic -α hard to explain; -η would be expected after *w. Not cognate with Latin āra (“altar”).

1242.t: From ὡς (hōs) + αὔτως (aútōs), originally written separately in Homer.
